Israel’s Elections: What’s at Stake? eschelhaas Thu, 10/15/2026 - 18:12 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List A Palestinian farmer walks past election banners near the Palestinian-owned olive groves in the village of Rantes near Ramallah, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on October 6, 2026. ZAIN JAAFAR / AFP Q&A / Middle East & North Africa 15 October 2026 16 minutes Israel’s Elections: What’s at Stake? Israelis will soon head to the polls for the first time since the 7 October 2023 attacks and the seismic events that followed. In this Q&A, Crisis Group experts look at what issues concern the voters and what change the balloting may bring. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Arabic English Arabic Related Tags Israel/Palestine What is happening? On 27 October, Israelis will head to the polls at a particularly fraught moment in the country’s history. The vote is the first since the deadly Hamas assault of 7 October 2023, which killed 1,318 Israelis and precipitated seismic events in Israel-Palestine and across the Middle East – not least Israel’s destruction of Gaza and killing of at least 74,000 of its people. The repercussions of this turmoil for Israeli electoral politics now wait to be seen. With Israel still entangled in several conflicts – including in the Palestinian territories, in Lebanon, in Syria and with Iran – and at the centre of increasingly passionate domestic political debates around the world, Israelis, Palestinians and millions of others will be watching closely. About a dozen political parties are expected to cross the proportional threshold (3.25 per cent of the national vote) needed to enter the parliament, or Knesset, which has 120 seats. Two main blocs – of nearly equal weight, according to polls – are facing off against each other. One is an alliance of hard-right parties dominated by Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister and head of the Likud Party. The other camp is led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff and head of Yashar (meaning “straight”, as in honest), a centre-right party he founded in 2025. A third group, made up of parties that represent Israel’s Palestinian Arab minority, is projected to capture a smaller but critical share of seats. Defining party platforms is an inexact science. The vertical axis reflects domestic issues; the horizontal, external ones (including occupied territories). Box size reflects poll projections of seat numbers. Sources: israel-polls-2026.pages.dev. Party positions are Crisis Group assessments, building on Peter Lintl’s framework for Israel’s 2022 election, “Israel’s Anti-liberal Coalition”, Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik, 27 January 2023 / CRISIS GROUP Notwithstanding nuances among the various parties, the 2026 contest is largely a battle between different right-wing approaches to governing an Israel that has all but consolidated its control of the Palestinian territories – ie, the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem. Questions that outsiders might expect to be at the centre of election debates, such as Israel’s almost 70-year occupation of these lands, preoccupy Israeli voters far less than internal issues, including the rule of law and relations between religion and state. That divergence raises complex questions about what change the world can expect to see after 27 October – and what is likely to stay the same. What are the chances of Netanyahu remaining in power? Significant, but it is too close to call. On one hand, the election comes at an especially tough time for Netanyahu. Poll numbers measuring his personal popularity and the degree of public trust he enjoys have been low for most of the period since 7 October 2023. His many years of domineering leadership – and in the view of former coalition partners, his corruption, manipulations and betrayals – have shrunk his pool of potential political allies. His Likud Party, the dominant force on the Israeli right since the 1970s, now polls lower than Eisenkot’s Yashar. Polls also show that given a choice between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, Israelis tend to favour the former general (who also garnered public sympathy after his son was killed in action in Gaza), over the sitting prime minister. For months, the parties that make up Netanyahu’s current coalition have together consistently polled well below the numbers needed for a 61-seat majority. A new hard-right party, Amcha Yisrael, led by former general Ofer Winter, could also be a handicap for Likud: it could draw votes away from Netanyahu’s party, but it could also “burn” votes, meaning render them irrelevant, since votes for smaller parties are discounted from the tally if they fail to cross the 3.25 per cent threshold. Yet Netanyahu, who turns 77 on 21 October, has long defied presumptions that his career has run its course. His skill at juggling crises is legendary; the latest ones include a lengthy trial for alleged corruption , widespread anger at his gradual overhaul of the judiciary, charges of failing to heed warnings ahead of the 2023 Hamas attack and then shirking responsibility for it, Israel’s sinking international reputation and an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court, not to mention an open-ended, seven-front war spanning the Middle East. Some of his opponents, recalling what he has done in past election campaigns, worry that the pugnacious prime minister may resort to tactics aimed at dividing his opponents. In particular, they fear he may try to discourage or intimidate would-be voters among Israel’s Palestinian Arab citizens. Some are also apprehensive that, should he become desperate, Netanyahu might launch a new military action, perhaps against Iran, in an attempt to postpone the election . Regardless of any such manoeuvres, the far-right, religious, pro-settler coalition led by the prime minister is strong. It has survived four turbulent years in power and still enjoys a firm base of support, including among young and first-time voters. True, the Netanyahu bloc has consistently polled well below a majority needed to form a coalition, and the anti-Netanyahu bloc – a disparate collection of right-wing, centrist and centre-left Jewish parties, as well as two lists of Palestinian Arab parties – represents a bigger proportion of the electorate in raw numbers. But several of the latter camp’s Jewish leaders have publicly sworn they would not form a government with the Arab parties, implying they might even be loath to rely on these parties’ Knesset votes to bolster a minority coalition. With neither bloc able to reach a majority alone, the Arab parties look like kingmakers. But they will not join a Netanyahu-led coalition, and the anti-Netanyahu bloc is wary of inviting them into government. Source: Crisis Group estimates based on aggregate polling data up to 14 October. Some votes may be “lost” to parties that fail to reach the 3.25 per cent threshold. / CRISIS GROUP This reluctance to share power with Arabs is not new, but it has become a matter of political consensus since 7 October 2023. The Netanyahu camp’s repeated claim that its adversaries can only win by joining ranks with Arab parties is also a sign of how the far right now shapes the political climate: it appeals to anti-Arab prejudice to alarm voters and taunt opponents, as well as to trap them into possibly self-defeating commitments. The delegitimisation of any coalition that might include Arabs has increased Netanyahu’s chances of remaining as caretaker prime minister until another round of elections a few months later, not by winning, but by blocking the other side. What are the most important – and divisive – issues for Israeli voters? The elections are in part a referendum on Netanyahu, particularly on his responsibility (or lack thereof) for the 7 October 2023 events and his actions thereafter. Many Israelis blame him for a policy of accommodating Hamas’s rule in Gaza in the years leading up to the lethal attack, including the facilitation of Qatari financing; for reportedly ignoring warnings of an impending Hamas operation; for allegedly relegating Israeli hostages to the back burner among war priorities in Gaza; and for refusing to name an independent commission of inquiry into the intelligence and other failures that helped make the Hamas assault so deadly. Netanyahu’s supporters dismiss such charges as a political inquisition led by Israel’s “deep state” (which they allege includes judges and generals) along with left-leaning media and foreign-funded organisations. They defend the prime minister’s wars, arguing that he has smashed Hamas in Gaza and Hizbollah in Lebanon and (having persuaded the U.S. to join in) severely weakened the Islamic Republic of Iran, securing Israel’s uncontested regional primacy. The legacy of Netanyahu’s coalition, widely viewed as the most extreme in Israel’s history, is also at stake in that referendum. Since taking office in December 2022, the right-wing Likud and its harder-right partners have pursued an aggressive agenda of redesigning parts of the Israeli state, the occupation of the Palestinian territories and Israel’s regional surroundings. They have sought to weaken the judicial system as an institutional check (indeed the only remaining one) on the executive and legislature, at the same time as working to entrench government influence over Israeli media, tighten restrictions on civil society, extend religious laws and practices into various spheres of public life, and accelerate Israel’s de facto annexation of the West Bank. Meanwhile, they also stand accused of failing to support Jewish border towns affected by years of war, such as those near the Lebanese frontier, whose residents fled Hizbollah rocket fire and still consider it unsafe to return. Many Israelis who regard themselves as secular, socially liberal and advocates of mamlakhtiyut (meaning the primacy of the state over factional interests) view the government’s ambitions for extending its power as anathema. These critics accuse firebrand leaders such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir of endangering Israel’s democracy, its social cohesion and its image abroad. A fresh government unbeholden to the far right, they say, could help repair some of that damage. A dispute that encapsulates these multiple fissures concerns the conscription of Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) citizens into the Israeli army. Even as the Haredims’ share of Israel’s population grew from under 5 per cent in 1980 to nearly 15 per cent today, they continued to enjoy exemption from state service on religious grounds until 2024, when the Supreme Court overruled the exception. Two Haredi parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, which were formally part of Netanyahu’s coalition until mid-2025, sought to circumvent the ruling via new legislation that the prime minister promised to push. But they failed to reach an agreement that would pass the Knesset, as some members of the ruling coalition – including within Likud – favour universal conscription. In practice, most Haredi youths continue to dodge the draft. Opposition leaders ... dismiss partnering with Haredi parties unless they agree that their constituents should submit to the draft. The Haredim are deeply unpopular with many political factions. Opposition leaders, many of whom are secular or of military background, dismiss partnering with Haredi parties unless they agree that their constituents should submit to the draft. Pressure to enforce the law has mounted from exhausted army reservists whose lives have been disrupted by repeated call-ups over the last three years. The military has also repeatedly warned that it faces a personnel shortage, especially in light of the government’s demand that soldiers protect increasing numbers of settler outposts in the West Bank. For the 20 per cent of Israel’s citizenry who are Palestinian, the top issues are different. Many see blocking the far right as vital to protecting their precarious civil rights and to ensuring greater access to state resources, as well as to mitigating Israel’s worsening policies in the occupied territories. But most Arab voters also have a particularly urgent concern: restoring their personal safety amid an alarming surge in organised crime and gun violence in Arab towns, which has reached record levels under the watch of Ben-Gvir’s national security ministry and the police it oversees. The two Arab-led slates, the Joint List (made up of Hadash, which identifies as an Arab-Jewish socialist party; Ta’al, which describes itself as an Arab movement for renewal; and Balad, a Palestinian Arab nationalist party) and the Islamist Ra’am, in theory have the potential to become “kingmakers”. Neither the pro- nor anti-Netanyahu blocs will be able to reach a parliamentary majority without Arab support, either as part of a governing coalition or as outside votes to back a given coalition. But it is unclear how and to what extent such electoral clout can translate into collective gains when even most of Israel’s mainstream opposition reject partnering with them. The Arab parties themselves are not in lockstep; while Ra’am is seeking to join a coalition with only domestic concerns in mind, the Joint List stipulated that at least some demands relating to the occupied territories, such as a diplomatic pathway to a Palestinian state, must also be addressed in order for it to provide a “safety net” (ie, serve as external support) for a minority government. Is the conflict with the Palestinians playing a role in the elections? For the ruling parties, yes; for the opposition, barely. In addition to its war on Gaza, the Netanyahu government has spent its tenure hastening Israel’s de facto annexation of the West Bank and extending “Jewish sovereignty” through settlements, making the prevention of a Palestinian state its flagship goal. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a portfolio in the defence ministry, in particular has spearheaded efforts to advance de jure annexation. The Likud is promoting the slogan “Yamin o’ Falastin” (Hebrew for “ The Right or Palestine ”) to suggest that any alternative government would pave the way for Palestinian statehood, notably because it would depend on support from the Arab parties. Leading coalition figures loudly applaud the devastation of Gaza, with some others still promoting the expulsion of its people and the re-establishment of Jewish settlements in the strip. Opposition Jewish figures are less coherent or vocal on the topic, but by and large they do not call the settlement enterprise’s continuation into question. Some blast the government’s support for the more extremist settler agendas; virtually none supports Palestinian statehood, at least not in the near future; and many try to ignore the Palestinian question altogether. One possible exception is Avigdor Lieberman, a former defence minister and leader of the right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu, a party that largely represents Russian immigrants, and who proposes that Jordan assume responsibility for ruling Palestinians inside a truncated portion of the territory. The centre-left Democrats, led by reserve major general and parliamentarian Yair Golan, is perhaps the only Jewish party that openly supports a two-state solution, yet it conditions a Palestinian state on a host of caveats (such as maintaining long-term Israeli security control of the entire territory) and argues that in any case the time is not right for such a state to emerge. Only the two Arab lists consistently promote Palestinian rights and self-determination, though Ra’am largely relegates these issues to secondary importance in its campaign. One West Bank issue that has generated Israeli debate is mounting settler violence against Palestinians. One West Bank issue that has generated Israeli debate is mounting settler violence against Palestinians, with even Netanyahu condemning what he insists are “fringe groups”. What appears to concern Israel’s mainstream media and Jewish voters, however, is less the harm being done to Palestinians than the added burden being placed on Israel’s occupying army and the state’s resources. Many also lament the further blemishes on Israel’s international image. Next to nothing has been done to stop the attacks in practice, and official policies that more broadly immiserate West Bank Palestinians, such as economic strangulation , home demolitions and land expropriation, rarely elicit comment from the (non-Arab) opposition. In a late August interview, Eisenkot said the army had “lost its control” of the West Bank due to the Netanyahu government’s policies and its emboldening of settler vigilantes. He also criticised the push to build the controversial E1 settlement , which would split the West Bank in two, as a “mistake” that has angered Israel’s allies. In a more recent interview , he claimed that a Yashar-led government would not only curb the actions of what he has called “Jewish terrorists” but also evacuate all outposts considered illegal under Israeli law in the West Bank (under international law, all settlements on occupied territory are considered illegal). It is fair to assume that he might also freeze construction of E1. But Eisenkot has also described the two-state solution as “delusional” and stressed that “I very much believe in settlement in Judea and Samaria” (the biblical term that many Israelis use for the West Bank). Naftali Bennett – head of the Together slate, a former prime minister and past head of the Yesha settler council – is unapologetic about his support for annexing the West Bank’s Area C (ie, the part that the 1993-1995 Oslo accords left under full Israeli administrative and security control) and his rejection of Palestinian statehood. The same is true of opposition figure Lieberman, as well as two other prominent politicians, Benny Gantz and Yoaz Hendel, who have positioned themselves as unaligned with either bloc. The competing parties may differ over whether to prop up the Palestinian Authority with financial and security cooperation and who should govern Gaza, but these are peripheral rather than central disagreements. Vis-á-vis the Palestinians, the next Israeli government will assume power on a markedly different footing from when the current one was elected four years ago. In the interval, Israel has swallowed more territory and squeezed Palestinians into smaller cantons in both Gaza and the West Bank. It has razed cities and refugee camps and emboldened a settler movement that will likely remain feverishly active regardless of who is in power. There is now near-consensus among Israeli Jews about maintaining security control throughout the occupied territories – from the proverbial river to the sea. But while the far right wants to turbo-charge the settlement enterprise and turn up the heat on the Palestinians further, many Israelis would prefer to bracket the issue, reverting to policies that can manage the conflict on their terms rather than seeking a political agreement with the Palestinians. The latter approach kept the occupation out of sight and out of mind – but also kept its end out of reach. Such shades of difference could change the level of physical and economic violence meted out to Palestinians, which is no small matter. But they would barely touch the core of the occupation itself. Have Israel’s other military campaigns in the region – in Lebanon, Syria and Iran – influenced the domestic political scene? Surprisingly little. A majority of Jewish Israelis has consistently supported Israel’s wars, with tens of thousands of soldiers and reservists continuing to serve despite widespread disillusionment with Netanyahu’s government. Even when Israelis were forced into shelters for weeks on end during the present war with Iran, public support remained high. In many ways, the seven-front war of the past three years has simply accelerated Israel’s rightward shift. Such criticism as there is tends to demand a harder, not softer approach. The centrist opposition leader Yair Lapid, whose Yesh Atid party is running alongside Bennett on the Together slate, said Israel should not have stopped at assassinating Iran’s leadership but should have bombed its oil and gas facilities during the second phase of the war, which started in late February. Bennett, for his part, has made classifying Qatar as an enemy state a central talking point. In November 2024, days before a ceasefire was brokered between Lebanon and Israel, Gantz, an ostensibly centre-right former general, called on the military to bomb Lebanese government assets. What are the most likely outcomes? Barring a dramatic development, and assuming the most credible polls are largely correct, four plausible scenarios could emerge after election day: A hung parliament. Neither bloc wins a decisive parliamentary majority or ropes enough parties into supporting a minority government. This outcome is possible, for instance, if Eisenkot or his allies refuse to bring the Arab lists into the fold or to rely on their outside support. The result would be another round of elections. In this case, Netanyahu would stay on as caretaker prime minister, with his sitting coalition continuing to hold the reins of government for several months, pending a fresh vote. Yashar edges out Likud and forms a government drawn from the opposition. This scenario would likely require Eisenkot to partner in some fashion with the two lists that represent Palestinian citizens – perhaps as external backers, instead of coalition partners – with the principal aim of keeping Netanyahu and his bloc out of power. There is precedent for this arrangement (albeit in starkly different circumstances), such as when Arab parties gave outside support to Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin from 1992 until his assassination in 1995. But shifts in public opinion, especially after the 7 October 2023 attacks, make reliance on the Joint List in particular a politically fraught proposition. Parties or politicians break ranks. Following an inconclusive result, Eisenkot or Netanyahu could convince parties or individual Knesset members in the opposing bloc to defect and form a “national unity government”. There could be several permutations along these lines. For example, commentators have suggested that the opposition consider forming a government with Likud, excluding far-right parties such as Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit. Netanyahu himself has floated this possibility. Though it got broadly negative responses, there is recent precedent, albeit with mixed results. In 2020, Netanyahu persuaded Gantz, then his biggest rival, to join a coalition, causing Gantz’s Blue and White Party to split. The government dissolved only a few months later. A bloc defies the polls and clinches a parliamentary majority. This outcome is highly unlikely. It would mean that months of polls have been egregiously wrong, given that all have said neither bloc is close to winning 61 seats. A surprise could conceivably occur if several parties fail to cross the electoral threshold, thus “burning” a large share of votes, or if turnout for certain parties far exceeds expectations. Israel’s electoral system has always been prone to twists and turns, but the 2026 election’s result is arguably less predictable than usual. Dry numbers from various sources provide hints. An independent aggregator of opinion polls over recent months suggests that the chances of either bloc achieving an outright majority are well under 10 per cent. Online betting sites , which are a rough indicator of where investors put their money, give Eisenkot and Yashar slightly greater respective odds of becoming the next prime minister and largest party in the Knesset. Still, even in that scenario Eisenkot would have to decide whether to partner with Arab parties, a question he has skirted until now. The outcome may not be all that stable. Despite a reshuffling of parties and emergence of new personalities, and though the political spectrum as a whole has shifted further rightward, Israeli voters appear to be caught in the same deadlock that has largely held since 2019 – one that led Israeli voters to go to the voting booths five times in three years until the current government took office – and held onto it for four years. The recent uptick in international pressure on Israel’s West Bank policies – notably, the UK-led settlement trade ban in September – is unlikely to fundamentally shift Israeli views in the near term, though it may affect voter turnout for one side or the other. Many Israelis are distrustful or dismissive of foreign criticism, believing that outsiders do not understand their nation’s unique circumstances, are overly fixated on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict or harbour anti-Israeli or anti-Semitic views. That said, they are not oblivious to the threat of isolation. They know that Israel’s brutal Gaza war, its increasingly aggressive policies in the West Bank and the proliferation of Middle East conflicts have all come at a high reputational cost to Israel, not only harming its diplomatic standing but also affecting its citizens’ interactions with the outside world. The question is whether mounting outside pressure can constructively shift Israeli calculations on war and peace after election day – regardless of the coalition that emerges. On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 10/16/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 16 October 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 16 October 2026 IRAN Iranian attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz have surged in October to date, with more than two dozen vessels struck since the month began. Meanwhile, Washington is maintaining its blockade of Iranian ports while backing oil shipments along the Omani coast, where smaller tankers transfer cargo to larger vessels outside the strait. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick in Iranian strikes is an effort to counter a rebound in oil flows that showed Tehran’s grip on the Strait of Hormuz was weakening. Iran wants Washington to accept its proposed terms for a ceasefire that reopens the waterway in exchange for sanctions relief and an end to the U.S. blockade. But a diplomatic breakthrough appears less likely than the two sides setting off another escalatory spiral. An argument over allegations of harassment reportedly prompted hundreds of men from the neighbouring Sunni-majority town of Qalaat al-Madiq to rush into Suqaylabiyah, ransacking Christian shops, homes and other property. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the episode underscores persistent shortcomings in Syria's security architecture. State forces tend to react to such incidents rather than help prevent them. Largely drawn from the Sunni majority, these forces lack understanding of minority groups, whose trust in the new authorities is fast eroding. Until the government addresses those weaknesses, the risk of more such violence will remain high – particularly in diverse areas where tensions built over fourteen years of war are still raw. 27 March 2026 IRAN With the Middle East war in its fourth week, the Trump administration submitted to Tehran, via Pakistani mediators, what U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff described as a “fifteen-point action list that forms the framework for a peace deal”. The plan, among other things, would reportedly require that the Islamic Republic give up its capacity to enrich uranium, which it has previously refused to do. Iran has countered with its own list of demands, including that the U.S. withdraw from all its military bases in the Gulf, which Washington has dismissed out of hand. Meanwhile, the U.S. is sending more ground troops to the region. A negotiated end to the conflict seems out of reach for now, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, as each side thinks its wartime position remains favourable. More likely is a protracted standoff or, worse, a dramatic escalation. IRAQ Fresh hostilities erupted this week between the U.S. and Iraqi militias backed by Tehran. These groups belong to an umbrella institution, the Hashd al-Shaabi, that is formally under the aegis of the Iraqi military commander-in-chief, though some of them operate independently. Those aligned with Iran have launched several rockets at U.S. bases in Iraq and neighbouring countries. A retaliatory U.S. airstrike on the Hashd headquarters in Baghdad killed fifteen fighters and another on a military facility in western Iraq claimed seven more lives. Meanwhile, the peshmerga in Iraqi Kurdistan, who are friendly to Washington, said Iranian missiles hit one of their bases in Erbil, killing six. The Iraqi government protested the infringements upon its sovereignty. But it lacks the leverage to stop the deadly exchanges, says Crisis Group expert Lahib Higel. The country is also facing an impending fiscal crisis, as oil sales have declined steeply with the Strait of Hormuz mostly shut. SUDAN UN agencies issued statements Tuesday protesting a “sharp increase” in drone warfare that is taking a mounting civilian toll. At least 70 people were killed the previous day when drones hit a hospital in East Darfur. Patients, doctors and nurses were among the dead. Another 28 civilians were killed in drone strikes in North Darfur and North Kordofan Thursday. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says both main belligerents in Sudan’s war, the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), have stepped up their use of drones in an attempt to get an edge on the battlefield. Meanwhile, the risk of spillover into neighbouring countries is heightening, with the RSF taking a town on the Ethiopian border and fighting continuing on the Chadian frontier. 20 March 2026 CHAD - SUDAN A drone attack Wednesday killed seventeen people in Chad’s border town of Tine, including mourners gathered for a funeral and children playing nearby. The Chadian government accused the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan of launching the drone. In late February, the RSF had hit Chadian army positions in Tine, killing several Chadian soldiers. President Mahamat Déby ordered a total closure of the border with Sudan, which could have negative humanitarian consequences. The border has officially been closed since April 2023, but until now authorities have been allowing some refugees and aid shipments through. He also warned that Chad would retaliate for any further strikes on its territory, no matter who is responsible. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says Chad, which hosts around one million Sudanese refugees, increasingly risks getting drawn into the war in Sudan as fighting routinely spills across the border. IRAN Oil and gas prices soared and stock markets dived Thursday after Iran struck Qatar’s main natural gas facility, Ras Laffan. The Iranian attack came a day after Israel hit Iran’s South Pars gas field, one of the world’s largest. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these tit-for-tat attacks on hydrocarbon infrastructure signal a new phase in the conflict, now entering its fourth week, as a global energy crisis looms and Gulf Arab states are increasingly caught in the crossfire, with Saudi Arabia warning of military action against Iran as these states’ patience wears thin. NIGERIA Multiple suicide bombings Monday killed at least 26 people and injured over a hundred in Maiduguri, capital of Nigeria’s Borno state. The attacks mark the second deadliest incident in Maiduguri in the past five years. No group has yet claimed responsibility. The bombings come amid a surge of violence in the country’s north east, with both Boko Haram and the Islamic State-West Africa Province, an ISIS affiliate, launching lethal raids. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says the latest attacks indicate that these insurgencies may again be gaining momentum. The Nigerian government and its foreign partners should step up efforts to counter the new challenge and halt rising insecurity in other parts of the country. 13 March 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Drone strikes killed several people Tuesday night in Goma, capital of North Kivu province in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, including a French woman working with UNICEF and at least two other residents. The M23 rebels who hold the city blamed the Congolese government for the attacks. Kinshasa said an investigation is under way. Despite a formal ceasefire in their conflict, both the Congolese government and the M23 (backed by Rwandan troops) have been acquiring drones as a means of getting around enemy defences. Tuesday’s attacks, along with another in February that killed M23 spokesperson Willy Ngoma, mark a dramatic escalation in the conflict’s aerial warfare. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says Kinshasa, which has purchased Chinese and Turkish drones, is determined to use its new arsenal to show the rebels they are not safe in their bastions. But with civilian casualties mounting, the government’s growing reliance on drones could backfire by costing it international support. Having flexed its muscles, Kinshasa would be well advised to return to the diplomatic arena, pressing for Rwandan withdrawal from the country and returning to negotiations with the M23 with a stronger hand. IRAN Amid a widening Middle East conflict sparked by U.S.-Israeli strikes that began two weeks ago, the Islamic Republic effected only the second transition in its most senior post since the 1979 revolution that brought it to power. Mojtaba Khamenei has taken up the position of Supreme Leader, which his father Ali held from 1989 until his death on 28 February in the war’s opening salvo. The U.S.-Israeli campaign has continued unabated, doing significant damage. Iran has responded with drone and missile strikes in the Gulf and brought traffic in the Strait of Hormuz to a crawl. The first official statement attributed to the younger Khamenei was defiant in tone, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, highlighting the Iranian regime's desire to project continuity under duress, vis-à-vis both its foreign adversaries and its domestic opponents. But that ambition could be short-lived if Khamenei is targeted amid the hostilities or outmanoeuvred by other players in the regime's upper echelons. Many Iranians, meanwhile, are despairing at a leadership transition that so far promises more of the same. LEBANON Israel’s latest military escalation in Lebanon continued to wreak havoc this week. Since 2 March, when Hizbollah fired rockets toward Israeli territory for the first time in over a year, Israel has ramped up aerial bombardment, including of the capital Beirut, and forced hundreds of thousands to flee their homes. It has also sent more troops into southern Lebanon, with a view to establishing what it calls a “security zone” there. While Israel retains military superiority over Hizbollah, the Shiite party-cum-militia has put up a fight. On Wednesday, it launched a barrage of 100 rockets across the border, which triggered an especially brutal sequence of Israeli air raids. Crisis Group expert David Wood says neither of the belligerents appears ready to stop, even as Lebanese leaders scramble to find a diplomatic off-ramp. Already, the Lebanese public has paid a horrific price: the death toll has climbed to almost 700, and thousands more have seen their homes and communities destroyed. 6 March 2026 IRAN The U.S. and Israel launched massive airstrikes on Iran Saturday, hitting military installations and killing senior leaders, including Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. In retaliation, Iran fired missiles and drones at Israel, as well as U.S. bases and commercial infrastructure in Gulf states. The conflict's reverberations have quickly spread from the Indian Ocean to the eastern Mediterranean. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Tehran looks prepared for a drawn-out confrontation, betting that it can steadily raise the psychological and economic costs to its adversaries, while maintaining cohesion at the top of the political system despite Khamenei’s demise. The U.S.-Israeli campaign appears open-ended, with no clear objective yet defined. Airstrikes can substantially degrade Iran's military capabilities but are unlikely to dislodge the regime, and even if they did, state collapse in Iran would risk unleashing far wider regional disorder. AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Border clashes continued this week after Pakistan declared “open war” with Afghanistan last Friday. The declaration followed Taliban retaliatory cross-border attacks after Pakistani airstrikes on purported Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) targets in Afghanistan on 21 February. Pakistan then carried out another series of strikes on 27 February, including in Kabul. Islamabad accuses Taliban authorities of sheltering the TTP, which has stepped up attacks in Pakistan. Kabul denies it. According to the UN, the latest fighting has killed dozens of civilians in Afghanistan and displaced tens of thousands, with reports also indicating civilian casualties in Pakistan. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says a drawn-out conflict serves neither side's interests. Outside actors should press Islamabad and Kabul to de-escalate. ECUADOR The U.S. Southern Command said Tuesday Ecuadorian and U.S. forces had begun operations to curb organised crime in Ecuador. They first went after the Colombian armed group Comandos de la Frontera, which is active along the Colombian border. Ecuador’s military says the operations will continue indefinitely. While details are classified, news reports indicate that the U.S. played an advisory role, without putting troops on the ground. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says such cooperation is not new, but the latest announcement signals deeper U.S. involvement. Security ties have deepened as President Daniel Noboa aligns with the Trump administration’s preference for using military force to combat drug trafficking. 27 February 2026 CHAD - SUDAN Chadian authorities Monday announced the immediate closure of the country’s border with Sudan. The decision followed what N’Djamena described as “repeated incursions” linked to Sudan’s war, after clashes around the Sudanese border town of Tina involving the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and militias aligned with Sudan’s army. Chad said the border would remain closed until further notice, while allowing humanitarian exemptions, including for refugees and returnees, as well as approved aid deliveries. Crisis Group expert Charles Bouëssel says N’Djamena should maintain vital cross-border aid and preserve trade that sustains displaced populations. It should also ensure that security and disarmament operations in the east are conducted with restraint and impartiality to contain intercommunal tensions and prevent Chad from being drawn further into Sudan’s war. CUBA Cuban authorities Wednesday accused ten people on a U.S.-registered speedboat carrying weapons and tactical gear of attempting infiltration of Cuban territory with “terrorist intentions”. Border guards shot four people dead and wounded six others aboard the boat after its occupants allegedly opened fire. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any U.S. involvement and said Washington would investigate the facts independently. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the incident comes amid already high tensions between Havana and Washington, after the U.S. halted fuel imports coming into Cuba, exacerbating a severe energy crisis on the island, in hopes of pushing the Cuban authorities to negotiate an economic and political opening. SYRIA ISIS released an audio statement last weekend denouncing Syria’s interim government and calling for a renewed campaign against its forces. The jihadist group has since claimed responsibility for several attacks on Syrian army personnel in the northern and north-eastern parts of the country. These developments follow last month’s reported mass escape from the al-Hol camp, which held over 20,000 detainees, many of them relatives of suspected ISIS fighters. Some of these people got away as security broke down during an offensive led by Damascus on the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the closure of the camp compounds an already risky convergence. With the SDF sidelined, U.S. forces withdrawing from Syria and the new government’s security apparatus still finding its feet, ISIS seems to be seeking an opening to resume its insurgency. 20 February 2026 MATERNAL MORTALITY The World Health Organization released a study Tuesday showing that nearly two thirds of maternal deaths worldwide occur in countries wracked by conflict or instability. Crisis raises the risks associated with pregnancy, the report finds, though health services in conflict-affected places are generally already scarce. Some countries, such as Colombia and Ethiopia, have made progress in reducing maternal mortality through partnerships with NGOs with expertise in service provision in remote areas. But now aid cuts have put such programs in jeopardy, says Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing, even as women are dying in childbirth at alarming rates. Donor funds still available should be directed toward bolstering community-based health services, particularly in war zones, through such cost-effective means as midwifery. NIGERIA The Nigerian government announced Tuesday that the U.S. will dispatch 100 additional military personnel to assist in fighting jihadist groups in the northern part of the country. This deployment comes amid deadly attacks that killed 56 people in Niger state last weekend and 34 others in Kebbi state on Wednesday. These raids are part of a broader surge of violence that has claimed over 250 lives across north-central and north-western Nigeria in the past month. Hundreds more people have been abducted. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says jihadists and other armed groups are growing stronger in these regions and elsewhere, by exploiting gaps in rural and border security as government forces become increasingly overstretched. The U.S. aid notwithstanding, the government needs to urgently improve its response, including by expediting measures outlined under the “nationwide security emergency” President Bola Tinubu declared last November. U.S. - IRAN Iranian and U.S. delegations convened in Geneva Tuesday for talks about Tehran’s nuclear program, the second round of such negotiations this month. In parallel, the Islamic Republic’s foreign minister met with the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency for technical discussions. Both Iran and the U.S. noted a measure of progress, as did the Omani mediators, even as Washington continues to ramp up its deployment of military assets to the Middle East. But the gaps between the sides are still wide, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, even as regards what a possible agreement would cover. The negotiators have yet to wrestle with matters of substance. Tehran and Washington are aware of the high risks of failure, as well as the costs that fresh hostilities would bring. Yet the pace of diplomacy is lagging as momentum builds for confrontation. 13 February 2026 BANGLADESH The Bangladesh Nationalist Party won a landslide victory Thursday in the country’s first national elections since the 2024 ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whose Awami League was barred from contesting the vote. A concurrent referendum on the July Charter – a set of reforms negotiated by all the participating parties over the last year – passed by a wide margin. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says the turnout and referendum result reflect the credibility of both the election and the reform process in the eyes of most Bangladeshis. The incoming government will face daunting challenges, however, such as getting Bangladesh’s ailing economy back on track and improving security. ERITREA-ETHIOPIA Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of deploying its troops into Ethiopian territory Saturday to conduct joint manoeuvres with Ethiopian rebels along the border. In response, Asmara said Ethiopia had fabricated evidence for this charge, asserting that it has “no appetite for or desire to engage in meaningless acrimony”. Crisis Group expert Magnus Taylor says this latest confrontation comes shortly after renewed clashes between Ethiopia and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front’s armed wing, which Addis Ababa alleges has formed a secret pact with Eritrea. More fighting could be in the offing if efforts to de-escalate tensions fail. WEST BANK Israel’s security cabinet Sunday approved measures that further cement Israeli control of the occupied West Bank, with the explicit goal of pre-empting the establishment of a viable Palestinian state. The move reflects an Israeli plan not only to annex all the Israeli settlements in the rural West Bank, but also to further limit what is left of nominal Palestinian autonomy and displace Palestinians from more built-up areas. Absent action that conditions trade and aid to Israel on policy changes, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein, international support for a two-state solution increasingly rings hollow. The annexation drive also undermines the Trump administration’s twenty-point plan for Gaza. 6 February 2026 GAZA Israel carried out strikes across the Gaza Strip Wednesday, killing at least 24 Palestinians. The Israeli army claimed it was targeting a Hamas commander and responding to fire upon its troops, but civilians accounted for most of the casualties. Humanitarian needs also remain acute amid aid shortfalls; the Rafah crossing with Egypt has opened, after a long wait, but deliveries are still tightly restricted. PAKISTAN Police backed by soldiers reportedly killed more than 200 Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) fighters in raids throughout Balochistan, a south-western province next to Afghanistan, over the course of this week. The operations followed a rash of BLA attacks on police stations, military installations and residential areas that claimed 50 lives (33 civilians and 17 state personnel) over the weekend. Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban of harbouring the BLA high command, which they also say gets financial and logistical assistance from Pakistan’s arch-rival India. Crisis Group Executive Vice President Richard Atwood says the high death toll among the Baloch separatist insurgents shows that authorities planned the raids carefully, with a view to keeping civilians out of the crossfire. U.S. - COLOMBIA Presidents Donald Trump and Gustavo Petro met at the White House Tuesday after months of heated rhetoric prompted by disputes over issues such as migration, counter-narcotics cooperation and the 3 January U.S. raid grabbing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. The U.S. has dispatched additional naval assets, airpower and defensive systems to the Middle East. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. How War is Reshaping Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” eschelhaas Fri, 10/16/2026 - 18:13 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Iranians commute past a billboard depicting slain Lebanese Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah and Iran's slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in Tehran on September 27, 2026. ATTA KENARE / AFP Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 16 October 2026 12 minutes How War is Reshaping Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” Three years of hostilities have transformed Tehran’s network of allies in the Middle East. The Islamic Republic is now relying more heavily on itself, while adapting its relationships with partners whose diminished military utility has not necessarily reduced its commitment to their protection. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Hamidreza Azizi Senior Analyst, Iran https://x.com/HamidRezaAz Related Tags Iran Israel/Palestine Lebanon Syria Developments since 7 October 2023, when Hamas staged its deadly attacks on southern Israel, have transformed Iran’s network of state and non-state allies in the Middle East, as well as their role in Tehran’s military planning and deterrence posture. The weakening of Hamas and Hizbollah at Israel’s hands in the last three years, the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in Syria in December 2024 and, above all, the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran launched in February have altered the vectors of Iranian influence. Together, these events have exposed the limits of an Iranian strategy that had relied chiefly on regional partners to deter adversaries and keep any armed confrontation away from Iran itself. Instead, Tehran now places greater weight on capabilities under its direct control: missiles, drones and the ability to obstruct traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. This evolution does not mean that the “ axis of resistance ”, as Iran calls its collection of allies, has lost all relevance. Rather, it means that axis members are now assuming different functions and that Tehran is approaching them differently. Yemen’s Houthis have gained particularly significant strategic value for Iran because their ability to threaten Red Sea shipping complements Tehran’s leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf. In Iraq, major Shiite factions also remain important political partners, even as Tehran increasingly turns to smaller armed groups to conduct military operations. Overall, the result is a more fragmented network in which heightened local autonomy among Iran’s non-state partners coexists with tighter Iranian control of select cells and smaller armed organisations. Nor is a weaker “axis of resistance” necessarily synonymous with diminished Iranian commitment to its partners. Hizbollah’s lesser contribution to Iranian deterrence, for example, has not reduced Tehran’s determination to protect the Lebanese Shiite movement. To the contrary, Iran has shown itself more willing to use force in Hizbollah’s defence; it also has conditioned reaching a deal terminating its hostilities with the United States on an end to Israel’s campaign in Lebanon. In other terms, Iran still may be drawn into conflicts on its regional partners’ behalf, even as they have become less capable of shielding it from attack. From the Levant to Maritime Chokepoints Prior to October 2023, Iran’s Middle East strategy centred on the Levant . Syria under Assad’s rule was the linchpin, the only Arab state allied with Iran, which provided it with substantial benefits: a land corridor linking Iran and its Iraqi Shiite partners to Hizbollah; proximity to Israel’s borders; and a logistical hub that enabled Tehran to project its influence to the eastern Mediterranean seaboard. In June 2024, Yahya Rahim Safavi , a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps who was then military adviser to Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, likened Iran’s reach through the axis to that of the ancient Persian empire under Cyrus and Xerxes. The advantages of alliance with Assad explain why, over a decade of civil war in Syria, Tehran defended his regime at significant cost. Hizbollah fighters also helped the regime a great deal, battling both its domestic opponents and ISIS. Hizbollah was useful in another important way, offering Tehran a means of threatening Israel from adjacent territory, thus ostensibly deterring it from direct strikes on Iran itself. If Assad’s Syria was a linchpin of the Islamic Republic’s Middle East strategy, the Shiite movement in Lebanon was a principal engine. [Assad’s fall] deprived Iran of its sole Arab state partner and disrupted its supply line to Hizbollah. This arrangement has suffered severe damage since October 2023 , when Hamas – apparently taking even Iran’s leadership by surprise – attacked Israel. The Gaza campaign that Israel launched in response dealt the axis a first blow, although Iran’s relationship with the Palestinian group has never been on par with those it has enjoyed with its other affiliates. Assad’s fall – indirectly part of the chain of events triggered by the Hamas attacks – was far more consequential. It deprived Iran of its sole Arab state partner and disrupted its supply line to Hizbollah. After Hizbollah entered the post-2023 fray, Israeli counter-attacks also inflicted substantial losses on the Lebanese movement’s leadership and military assets, while causing significant death, destruction and displacement in the country. As a result, other Lebanese factions began issuing more urgent calls on Hizbollah to disarm. The setbacks reinforced one another: rebuilding a degraded Hizbollah was a far more daunting task without the Syrian channel that had previously sustained it. These losses notwithstanding, Tehran has yet to forsake the Levant. Hizbollah still has a strong, institutionalised relationship with Iran, significant political weight in Lebanon and the capacity to regroup, at least in part. The Israeli incursions into southern Syria following the Assad regime’s demise may also have benefits for Iran. The Islamic Republic may be banking on local resistance to Israel eventually creating openings for renewed Iranian influence in Syria, though this prospect remains uncertain. For now, Iran has turned its attention to an arena closer to its borders where it retains heftier clout. On 8 June, Esmail Qaani , commander ofthe Revolutionary Guards’ overseas operations arm, the Qods Force, described an emerging “security belt” stretching from the Gulf to the Red Sea. When compared to Safavi’s formulation two years prior, the phrase captures a shift in emphasis from the Levant to the maritime routes linking the Gulf to the western Indian Ocean, a theatre in which Iran’s sway comes more directly from its own place on the map. The Islamic Republic requires neither an allied state nor a non-state partner to project power in the Strait of Hormuz; it can station missiles and drones nearby or even deep inland to threaten naval or commercial vessels in these waters. Tehran’s influence over maritime routes upon which states near and far depend for trade in oil, gas and other vital commodities is boosted by its partnership with the Houthis, who can fire at ships passing in either direction through the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab. Though it no longer serves as a land bridge for arms transfers to Syria and Lebanon, Iraq nonetheless plays an important part in this changing landscape. In particular, it is a locus for coordination between the Houthis and Iraqi armed groups , as well as between the Qods Force and Iraqi groups that have conducted attacks on Gulf Arab states. A More Fragmented Network The shift in Iran’s primary focus from the Levant to the seas has gone hand in hand with organisational changes. Under its late commander Qassem Soleimani, the Qods Force was the principal coordinator of “axis of resistance” activities. Since the U.S. killed Soleimani in January 2020, the Qods Force has not played the same role. Subsequent wars and leadership losses, both within the Revolutionary Guards and among its partners, further discombobulated command structures and impaired joint military operations. As a result, Iran has had to adapt its relationships with groups whose military capabilities and domestic constraints themselves have changed. It has increasingly been compelled to work through smaller groups or selected elements of established organisations. This trend has been most evident in Iraq. As the years passed after Saddam Hussein’s ouster, older Shiite political movements acquired key government positions and economic interests, thus becoming more beholden to popular constituencies. As a result, they are now more hesitant to engage in military action that risks provoking retaliation or eroding their standing. This reluctance was apparent early in the present U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, when several major Iraqi Shiite armed groups declined to mobilise on Tehran’s behalf. Iran had to rely on smaller, less prominent ones – drawn from the self-styled Islamic Resistance in Iraq – to come to its aid. Iraqi sources speak of a network of clandestine cells established by the Revolutionary Guards and operating outside established militias’ command structures that reportedly has been responsible for attacks on Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. These nimbler, smaller groups offer Tehran several advantages. They require fewer resources, they can conceal their affiliations and they can ignore the political constraints holding back their larger counterparts. Their greater ideological cohesion also arguably makes them easier for Tehran to direct. More institutionalised Iraqi Shiite groups remain important to Tehran, notwithstanding their reticence regarding military action in Iran’s defence. But their role has shifted: they are useful principally because they help Iran preserve influence in the country as well as the political space in which smaller armed groups are free to operate. Iran’s changing relationship with Hizbollah illustrates another type of adjustment to similar pressures. Though the movement retains a substantial organisation that helps Tehran sustain influence in Lebanon, Hizbollah’s military actions increasingly resemble those of a guerrilla group – quick-hitting raids that leave the group less vulnerable to Israeli airstrikes and intelligence penetration. Its use of first-person-view drones – drones using a live video feed from an onboard camera – to attack Israeli forces in southern Lebanon showcased the effectiveness of inexpensive technology, even as the movement has lost its more sophisticated capabilities. An Iranian expert with ties to both the Revolutionary Guards and Hizbollah told Crisis Group that Qods Force commanders have been directly involved in this revamping, including efforts to work through smaller units and help Hizbollah fighters adopt more agile tactics. Deterrence Moves Closer to Home, but the Axis Remains Important These changes reflect a broader reassessment of Iran’s deterrence posture. Its earlier approach heavily relied on the concept of “ forward defence ” ensured by regional partners, supplemented by the threat of direct retaliation from its own territory. The “axis of resistance” gave the Islamic Republic strategic depth , discouraging its adversaries from attacking it and keeping conflict distant from its borders. Only if that first layer of protection were to fail were Iranian missiles and drones to be used to shoot back. The past three years of war have starkly exposed the limits inherent in this arrangement. Iran’s regional network did not prevent direct attacks on the country – whether the major exchanges with Israel in 2024, the surprise Israeli attack in June 2025 or the more substantial confrontation with the U.S. and Israel beginning in February. As the deterrence value of axis partners dropped, Tehran was compelled to place greater weight on its own capabilities: missiles, drones and geographical leverage. If military setbacks have transformed the role played by the axis, they have not eliminated its utility to Iran. Yet, if military setbacks have transformed the role played by the axis, they have not eliminated its utility to Iran. Though the axis as a whole no longer serves as the primary foundation of Iran’s deterrence, decision-makers in Tehran believe that certain partners can play important roles in particular circumstances as they magnify Iran’s own capabilities and geographical leverage. Their experience during the present conflict with the U.S. has only bolstered this conviction. The Houthis have attained particular importance in the Islamic Republic’s thinking, which helps explain reports that Tehran has provided them with both guidance and military assistance. Tehran’s efforts in July to establish direct flights to Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen illustrated the multidimensional nature of this support: the flights both challenged restrictions imposed by Yemen’s internationally recognised government and Saudi Arabia on Houthi rule and reportedly carried Revolutionary Guards commanders, military advisers and missile- and drone-related equipment. Hizbollah, too, has retained its usefulness for Tehran. The movement attacked Israel following February’s U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, forcing Israel to contend with an additional front and placing further demands on its air defences. True, that supporting role was a far cry from the crucial deterrent function the movement was intended to play, a reflection of its diminished capabilities. Iranian officials have nevertheless continued to frame their confrontation with the U.S. and Israel as extending to Iran’s Middle East partners, Hizbollah in particular. In June, in a remarkable role reversal, Iran launched missiles at Israel in response to its campaign against Hizbollah, thereby marshalling its own forces in defence of its partner rather than the other way around. Moreover, it conditioned its acceptance of the (short-lived) 17 June memorandum of understanding halting hostilities with the U.S. on cessation of Israeli attacks in Lebanon: the opening clause explicitly included Lebanon in the ceasefire and affirmed Lebanese sovereignty and territorial integrity. Israel persisted with its offensive, however, including at Ali al-Taher , a strategic Hizbollah position in southern Lebanon where Israel besieged (and, in mid-September, demolished) an underground command and weapons complex. To Iranian officials, who had reportedly sent warnings that any such act would provoke a “forceful” response, the demolition was a reminder that Iranian threats of renewed missile attacks were an insufficient deterrent. Still, Iran’s stance showcased its commitment to axis members whose military utility has faded but not been erased. Decades of institutional ties, ideological affinity and investment help explain Iran’s approach. Decades of institutional ties, ideological affinity and investment help explain Iran’s approach. According to Iranian experts interviewed by Crisis Group, several members of the security establishment regard Hizbollah’s survival in particular as being closely tied to Iran’s own security, giving the relationship a significance that extends beyond the movement’s immediate military capabilities. This outlook has surfaced in public debates. In a January 2025 interview published by Iran’s Strategic Council on Foreign Relations, former diplomat Hadi Seyyed Afghahi argued that pressure on militant groups in Iraq, Lebanon and Yemen was aimed at “Iran and, more generally, the Shiites of the region”. Therefore, Tehran could not remain indifferent to these groups’ fate. Likewise, in December 2025, Ali Samadzadeh , an analyst with close ties to the regime, argued that Iran should be prepared to intervene militarily if Israel attacked Hizbollah, describing an assault on Lebanon as a prelude to renewed war with Iran. Defending regional partners, in this view, is part and parcel of protecting Iran itself. In short, where Tehran regards a partner as key to its own security, the fact that the partner has been weakened arguably – and perhaps paradoxically – provides Iran with added reason to intervene on its behalf. Efforts to curb Iranian influence by targeting allied groups may therefore draw Tehran into conflicts – a marked departure from the role these groups once played in shielding the Islamic Republic from direct involvement in hostilities. The extent of Iranian involvement is likely to depend on the particular relationship in question and the risks and costs inherent in intervention. But the bottom line is that its partners’ diminished military capabilities will not necessarily reduce Iran’s exposure to, or participation in, their respective conflicts. A Shifting Picture After three years of hostilities involving Iran’s partners and, since February, Iran itself, the “axis of resistance” is neither down nor out, but it is not what it once was, either in the function it serves or in Tehran’s relationship to its various members. The changes have been manifold. First, some of its members’ military capabilities have been significantly degraded. Secondly, direct confrontation with the U.S. and Israel has revealed the groups’ limited deterrent value and their inability to keep conflict away from Iranian territory. Finally, and partly as a result of their lessened status, they have come under growing domestic political, economic and security pressure, hindering their ability to directly participate in confrontations involving the Islamic Republic. These changes do not rule out these groups’ continued close operational ties to Tehran; nor do they mean an end to Iran’s commitment to their protection. But, together, they constrain the groups’ freedom of action. As a result, the focus of the Islamic Republic’s strategic doctrine has pivoted from allied non-state actors toward its own capabilities. This adjustment undoubtedly has preserved Iran’s ability to project power in its neighbourhood. But it does not come without serious risk, insofar as it has led Tehran to more directly bear the costs and dangers of confrontation. The Islamic Republic may well find ways to manage the consequences of its partners’ weakened clout by coming to their aid when they are endangered, giving them breathing space to regroup and using its own military assets to deter its foes, including by ensuring that others – notably Gulf Arab states – suffer the consequences of Middle East war. In so doing, Iran hopes to discourage future attacks. But this approach also risks deepening hostility among its neighbours, potentially encouraging closer security cooperation among Iran’s adversaries and heightening the very pressures Tehran seeks to reduce. Kazakhstan Women Need Action on Domestic Violence. Click to expand Image Participants at the international Women's Day rally in Almaty, Kazakhstan, March 8, 2022. © 2022 Stanislav Beketov During its October 6 review by the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), Kazakhstan pledged new legislation to make domestic violence a standalone crime – a timely commitment. Now the government should turn words into action. On September 23, Zhazira Adauova, a mother of two, died after her ex-husband stabbed her 16 times in Astana, Kazakhstan’s capital. Zhazira’s family told the media she had repeatedly reported threats and violence to police. Four former police officers are under investigation for alleged negligence in handling her case. Elvira Erkebayeva, from western Kazakhstan, endured two decades of domestic violence, including having boiling water thrown in her face. Instead of protecting her and holding her former husband accountable, authorities prosecuted Elvira in 2025 for allegedly conspiring to murder him because she wanted to “find a firearm.” As in manyother cases, Kazakh authorities failed to protect women who sought protection against further violence, even when they had obtained multiple protection orders. Perpetrators are often held accountable only after killing their victims. Kazakhstan no longer has a dedicated law on domestic violence, and the latest reforms still did not establish domestic violence as a standalone criminal offense. The 2009 Law on Prevention of Domestic Violence was repealed by the Law on Prevention of Offences, which entered into force in March addresses domestic violence within a broader prevention framework. The Kazakh delegation claimed during its CEDAW review that “enforcing zero tolerance for violence had become … the cornerstone of ongoing reforms,” and that in 2024 Kazakhstan had “intensified legal accountability for domestic … violence.” Yet CEDAW experts rightly questioned the effectiveness of existing measures, and the Committee’s Rapporteur for Kazakhstan underscored that domestic violence is still not a standalone criminal offence. Under CEDAW and the Committee’s General Recommendation No. 35, states must prevent, investigate, prosecute, and ensure accountability for gender-based violence. Kazakhstan should adopt reforms to make domestic violence a standalone offence, strengthen and improve enforcement of the protection order mechanism, ensure interventions are effective and perpetrators held accountable, and guarantee survivors’ access to justice and services. Kazakhstan’s international partners should press for these reforms. Accountability after a woman is dead is no substitute for timely protection and prevention. Kazakh authorities need to ensure that women in Kazakhstan receive meaningful protection and assistance before violence escalates or turns fatal.

Turkish Government Takes Over Independent TV News Channel. Click to expand Image Halk TV general news coordinator Serhan Asker gives an interview to media after the government takeover of the channel, a police raid on the premises, and the announcement of an arrest warrant against its owner and 16 others. Halk TV, Istanbul, October 14, 2026. © 2026 Adem Altan/AFP via Getty Images Police in Türkiye carried out a dawn raid on the widely watched, independent news channel Halk TV on October 14, signaling its takeover by a government-appointed administrator who promptly ordered the station to end its live broadcast. Halk TV is close to the main political opposition New Party (Yeni Parti). Its journalists have reported on the imprisonment and trial of Istanbul’s mayor, Ekrem İmamoğlu, government moves to split the opposition, and persistent allegations of corruption in the ruling party. The seizure of the channel is part of a wider effort by the government of Recep Tayyip Erdoğan to restrict Turkish citizens’ access to independent news sources that has involved pulling the plug on several TV news outlets, prosecuting and jailing journalists, and greatly escalating internet censorship. The Istanbul prosecutor’s office ordered the arrest of Halk TV’s owner on accusations of bribery, money laundering, and rigging tenders, along with 16 other people. As with other takeovers of media outlets, the financial crimes investigation provides a pretext for censorship. Halk TV will now be managed by the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund, a state body attached to the presidency, which has been used over the past 10 years to manage companies under governmental administration that are subject to criminal investigations. Halk TV continued to report on matters of pressing public interest until the last moment. An anchor was conducting an interview about an investment fund scandal implicating prominent figures in Erdoğan’s party moments before the administrators cut the live broadcast, leaving viewers instead with a scene from an old Turkish film. The takeover of Halk TV came on the very day that İmamoğlu took to the stand to begin his defense in the main politically motivated trial against him. The Turkish government’s steps to suppress and silence a TV station that broadcasts critical content violates not only the rights of the workers and journalists targeted, but the public’s right of access to information and to freedom of expression. Most people in Türkiye rely on television over other media for news coverage. Halk TV has been a critical voice in a country where broadcast news is increasingly monotone and government-aligned. The Turkish authorities should take immediate steps to reverse the takeover of the channel. A free, pluralistic media offering varied views and opinions is a cornerstone of a democratic society.

Cambodian Supreme Court Maximizes Sentence for Opposition Activist. Click to expand Image Cambodia’s Supreme Court, Phnom Penh, June 25, 2026. © 2026 Sopheng Cheang/AP Photo Cambodia’s Supreme Court on October 14 denied opposition activist Voeung Samnang’s request to serve his two sentences concurrently, meaning he will spend 11 years in prison. Samnang had been convicted on charges of “plotting an attack on the state” and received sentences of five and six years. The case illustrates the Cambodian government’s increased use of vague plotting charges to prosecute opposition activists and social media users and sentence them to long prison terms. Samnang had been a local commune official for the Cambodia National Rescue Party (CNRP), the opposition party dissolved by the government-controlled Supreme Court in 2017. He fled to Thailand in 2020 after charges were filed against him. In 2021, Thai police arrested him and forcibly returned him to Cambodia, alongside opposition activist Veourn Veasna, despite both being recognized as refugees by the United Nations refugee agency. Samnang was charged with plotting, convicted and sentenced to five years in prison in 2022 as part of a mass trial of 36 former CNRP leaders and supporters. While incarcerated, he was tried and convicted again in 2023 on additional plotting charges and sentenced to six years in prison. The ostensible evidence against him in both cases was Facebook posts related to the CNRP and his criticism of the government. Samnang’s wife, Teang Chenda, joined the “Friday Women,” a group of Cambodian women who held regular protests in the capital, Phnom Penh, to call for the release of their imprisoned husbands and sons. The Friday Women have faced harassment from Cambodian authorities during their public protests. Samnang’s case highlights the government’s unrelenting persecution of the political opposition ahead of next year’s local elections. Veasna, the man arrested alongside Samnang, was charged and convicted in a separate case. He later apologized to then-Prime Minister Hun Sen, joined the ruling Cambodian People’s Party, and was released from prison – part of the government’s systematic use of coerced confessions to discredit political opposition members and activists. Veasna later fled Cambodia and disavowed his defection to the ruling party.

Abusive Care Facility in Thailand Raises Broader Concerns. Click to expand Image A person lies in bed at a nursing home in Ayutthaya, Thailand, April 9, 2016. © 2016 Athit Perawongmetha/Reuters A care facility in Kanchanaburi, Thailand made headlines in early October when photos of conditions in the facility went viral, including images allegedly depicting metal cages that confine residents to their beds. Further investigation by the country’s Department of Health Service Support uncovered unsanitary conditions and overcrowding, as well as evidence that the facility had been treating residents with psychosocial disabilities (mental health conditions) without an appropriate license. The whistleblower, known as “Mae Phat,” appeared on television to recount her experiences at Sothornchai Nursing Home as a former resident, describing how she was involuntarily committed, forced to take medication, and physically restrained, often for hours at a time. Thai officials promptly ordered the facility’s closure as well as inspections of 1,203 facilities for older people nationwide. While the authorities have taken appropriate first steps, conditions at the facility have raised broader concerns about institutionalization, shackling, and the treatment of older people in Thailand. The United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs predicts that 28 percent of Thailand's population will be 65 or older within the next decade. Though Thailand has launched a community-based long-term care program for older people, responsibility for care falls under several government ministries. Ongoing shortages of qualified care and support workers as well as budgetary constraints leave many older people reliant on family care, which not all families can adequately provide. The Thai government should take this opportunity to reconsider its fragmented policies and commit to ensuring older people are treated with dignity and empowered to make decisions about their care and support. The government should develop and implement a comprehensive, time-bound deinstitutionalization plan for older people and people with disabilities, ensuring full access to community-based services and individualized support that would enable them to live independently and participate fully in their communities. The government should also establish a task force to conduct regular, unannounced visits to public and private institutions housing older people and people with psychosocial disabilities, assessing living conditions and conducting confidential interviews with residents and staff. This task force should also establish a hotline to receive and investigate reports of abuse and ensure accountability. Thailand should move beyond institutional care and guarantee everyone the support required to live independently in the community.

F1’s Rwanda Race Could Be Bad News for Rights. Click to expand Image Rwanda's President Paul Kagame delivers remarks during the announcement of the Formula 1 African Grand Prix at BK Arena in Kigali on October 13, 2026. © 2026 Jean Baptiste Nkurunziza/AFP via Getty Images Formula One’s decision this week to bring a Grand Prix to Rwanda in the early 2030s could be an important moment for Africa. The continent deserves more prominence on the global sporting calendar. But the 10-year agreement between Formula One and Rwanda also brings significant human rights risks. The Rwandan government’s repression means journalists and others who challenge the government’s relentlessly positive image of the country may be at risk prior to, during, and after race weekends. The Rwandan government has long targeted independent media and political opponents both within Rwandan and abroad, including through torture, unlawful military detention, enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings. Human Rights Watch has also documented how Rwanda’s authorities routinely round up and detain homeless people and street venders before large events. People detained in the capital Kigali are held in a large warehouse—labeled a “transit center”—until foreign visitors have left. For example, some of the city’s poorest and most marginalized people were locked up prior to an international conference in 2021. Rwanda, like other countries, has also used past high-profile sports deals and races to distract from its abysmal human rights record, a tactic known as “sportswashing.” Rwanda is currently the power behind the abusive M23 rebel group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and its military forces have been implicated in unlawful displacement, large-scale forced recruitment and arbitrary detention campaigns, and deaths of civilians in violation of international humanitarian law. Human Rights Watch wrote to Formula One on February 24 to ask how it is addressing the risks of sportswashing and of human rights abuses connected to its events, including regarding Rwanda’s bid to host an F1 Grand Prix. We’ve yet to receive a response.
